title: Young adults in northern England face 42% higher death rates

input.summary: The gap with southern England has more than tripled since 1981, despite falling death rates
input.evidence_text: North West health correspondent Published 1 hour ago Younger adults living in the north of England are 42% more likely to die than their counterparts in the South, according to new research A study by academics in Manchester and Liverpool found people in the North aged 25 to 49 faced a significantly higher risk of death than people of the same age living in southern England Researchers said deprivation was a major factor behind the gap and called for urgent action to tackle inequalities The Department of Health and Social Care said it was determined to reduce health inequalities and close the divide The research, by the University of Manchester, the University of Liverpool and Health Equity North, analysed deaths between 1981 and 2024 It found that while death rates fell overall, the gap between younger adults in the north and south more than tripled. title: Wigan council 'listening' as warehouse plans dropped

input.summary: Wigan Council said it had listened and "struck the right balance" between supporting growth and creating jobs
input.evidence_text: Wigan council 'listening' as warehouse plans dropped - BBC News Image source, Joanna Allsop Image caption, Members of the Save Our Astley and Boothstown Greenbelt at a summer protest By Kevin Fitzpatrick North West Published 1 hour ago A consultation's due to end on Wigan Council's plan for future development, with four sites potentially earmarked for warehouses being removed. It follows an outcry from residents over the construction of huge warehouses close to homes near Astley. The local authority said it had listened and "struck the right balance between supporting economic growth and job creation". Greenbelt campaigners and opposition councillors claimed they had forced the council to act. Councils must put together a local plan which identifies sites for housing and business development every decade or so and Wigan is in the process of updating its own. In the version under consultation, it has said four sites would not be taken forward. They include to the north of M6 junction 26, Moss Industrial Estate extension, Bridgewater West in Astley, and West of Winwick Lane in Lowton. The site being described as Bridgewater West is known locally as Higher Green and more than half a million sqaure feet of employment space was to have been built. Joanna Allsop from the Save Our Astley and Boothstown Greenbelt lives nearby and said; "It was just unbelievable that anyone could suggest that it could be anything other than Greenbelt." She said they are still concerned about its future, adding: "What we want is long-lasting protection. We want them to say that it is Greenbelt, not try to say that it's Greybelt." "There's been a lot of things that have made additional cost but we're really pleased to say that after we've revised the budget, it is now coming in on budget and there won't be any more increases." title: The Rainy City Hair Survival Guide | About Manchester

input.summary: Living in Manchester means accepting that rain is practically a permanent fixture on your calendar. That relentless North West damp air has an annoying habit of turning a fresh, polished morning style into a frizzy mess before you even manage to reach the tram stop. Navigating co
input.evidence_text: Living in Manchester means accepting that rain is practically a permanent fixture on your calendar. That relentless North West damp air has an annoying habit of turning a fresh, polished morning style into a frizzy mess before you even manage to reach the tram stop. Navigating co Hair naturally swells when it absorbs excess moisture from humid air, causing the outer cuticle layer to lift and create instant frizz. Keeping your strands properly hydrated while you are still in the shower stops them from seeking out and soaking up that damp outdoor air later Hair is at its most fragile state when wet because the internal structural bonds temporarily stretch. Yanking a standard comb or an aggressive paddle brush through damp strands creates micro-breakage that eventually shows up as frayed split ends a few weeks down the line. Adoptin Rough towel drying destroys smooth hair texture faster than almost anything else in your routine. Vigorously rubbing your head with a heavy bath towel roughens the cuticle layer instantly and triggers immediate frizz before you even reach for a hairdryer. A much smarter approach Whenever local humidity levels spike, using heat styling tools without proper pre-styling protection almost guarantees dull, damaged ends. Layering a lightweight leave-in conditioner or a thermal spray shields your hair before you blow-dry. Plenty of beauty enthusiasts regularly Rethinking how you treat damp hair makes an incredible difference in how well your style holds up outdoors. A few small, intentional tweaks to your daily routine will keep your hair looking healthy, smooth, and effortless every day of the week

input.evidence_text: Mental health is shaped as much by the places we live as by the care we receive. In Greater Manchester, from the terraces of Salford to the high streets of Stockport and the estates of Oldham, neighbours, schools, workplaces and local groups all play a part in helping people feel Support also needs to reach people in different ways, because no two experiences are the same. Some people find strength in a walking group, a community café or a peer support network, while others need specialist help for issues such as addiction, which can sit alongside anxiety Loneliness can affect anyone, including young adults, new parents, carers, older people and those who have recently moved to the area. Community centres, libraries, sports clubs, allotment groups and local arts projects can help people form meaningful relationships. Even small ge Greater Manchester has many diverse communities, and support should be culturally sensitive and accessible. This means providing information in different languages, recognising different family structures, and working with trusted local leaders who understand the needs of their n Stigma remains one of the biggest barriers to getting support. Communities can help by making conversations about mental health ordinary and respectful. Schools, colleges, workplaces and community groups can run awareness sessions, invite speakers with lived experience, and share It is important to use everyday language. People don’t always describe themselves as “depressed” or “anxious”; they may say they are exhausted, overwhelmed, angry, numb or unable to cope. Listening without rushing to offer solutions can make a real difference

Different regions have different strengths, assets and specialisms, and there was a strong view that greater collaboration between places could create bi Procurement and buying local also featured strongly. The discussion highlighted the role public sector buying power can play in supporting regional businesses, helping successful pilots move into commercial contracts and strengthening UK capability in areas such as AI and cyber There was also a broader conversation about sovereignty and the UK’s role internationally. title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.lead: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing.
input.summary: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised
input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. An exit takes a median of four years from a funding round

input.evidence_text: In 1965, The Sunday Times Magazine sent photojournalist John Bulmer north to document the region at a time when it was defined by industrial decline. But the images he returned with told a more complex story: shot in colour, they showed humanity and dignity alongside the hardship Sixty years later, photographer Simon Hill has retraced that journey. The conversation between their two bodies of work, now showing together at Jodrell Bank, builds a portrait of how much has changed since then and how much remains While Bulmer visited 16 locations across the North, Hill travelled to more than 50. From late 2024 to mid 2026 he crossed the historic seven counties from Newcastle to Liverpool, visiting former mining communities, coastal towns, city centres, remote landscapes, and the motorways In homage to Bulmer’s pioneering use of colour, much of Hill’s work was shot on Harman Phoenix 200, a contemporary colour film made in the North, and known for its unpredictable, textured qualities Bulmer’s North captured communities facing uncertain futures as the industries that defined them began to disappear. Hill’s is post-industrial, more diverse and still evolving. Former centres of heavy industry have become sites of cultural reinvention and technological growth. Bu Jodrell Bank feels a particularly fitting setting for work that’s fundamentally about time, distance and how we measure change. input.evidence_text: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. It runs every Sunday from February right through to December, drawing over 300 sellers and thousands of bargain hunters each week. Sellers can arrive and set up from 6:00 AM, with buyers welcomed in from 7:00 AM. Entry costs just £1 per car for buyers. Pitches for sellers are £14 for a car, £20 for a van and £3 for a trailer, with regular and corner pitches available on request. Bring exact change to keep the queue moving, and call organiser Andrew on 07470784644 for more details. Expect hundreds of stalls across the concrete hardstanding pitches, so it goes ahead in most weather. On-site you'll find a 5-star catering service, doughnuts and coffee, ice cream and desserts, a meat auction, fresh fruit and veg, plants, and retro sweet stalls. The sale is dog-friendly, has male and female toilets, ample parking, and kids' rides and bouncy castles to keep little ones entertained.
